report:
The evidence does not support "no" — the correct answer is **yes**, denosumab (Prolia) does reduce vertebral fracture risk, and this is one of the most robustly demonstrated effects of the drug in osteoporosis treatment.

**Evidence:**

The pivotal **FREEDOM trial**, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of ~7,800 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found that denosumab (60 mg every 6 months) reduced the 3-year cumulative incidence of new vertebral fractures to 2.3% versus 7.2% with placebo — a relative risk reduction of about 68% (risk ratio 0.32, p<0.001) (https://www.mdedge.com/obgmanagement/article/65217/gynecology/osteoporosis/page/0/1; https://www.cfp.ca/content/57/4/438). The same trial also showed reductions in hip fracture (~40%) and nonvertebral fractures. This benefit has been confirmed in extension studies out to 10 years, with sustained anti-fracture efficacy and continued BMD gains (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799550/). A systematic review of denosumab trials likewise reports a 68% reduction in vertebral fracture risk versus placebo (https://www.reumatologiaclinica.org/en-denosumab-for-treatment-osteoporosis-a-articulo-S1699258X12001787).

**Important caveat:** The benefit is contingent on continued treatment. Discontinuing denosumab causes a "rebound" surge in bone turnover, and post-hoc analyses of FREEDOM and its extension found an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures after stopping the drug, particularly in patients with prior vertebral fractures (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5915244/). This means clinicians must plan for transition therapy (e.g., a bisphosphonate) after stopping denosumab.

**Conclusion:** While denosumab carries risks upon discontinuation, the well-established, high-quality randomized trial evidence clearly shows it *does* reduce vertebral fracture risk during active treatment — the opposite of "no."
